Aruṇagirināthar
------------------------------------------
A work, Tiruppugaḷ containing सोउल्-stirring hymns on Lord Muruga (Subrah-maṇya), is very popular in Tamil Nadu. The author अरुणगिरिनाथर्, a Śaiva saint, lived in the 15th century. It is said that he had an infamous birth and led a riotous life in his youth. A simple remark from his own sister caused such an intense remorse that he tried to commit सुइचिदे by jumping from the high tower of the temple. However, God saved him in a miraculous way. Thenceforth he dedicated his life for God. Sublime poetry welled forth from his heart as a result of divine grace showered on him. Some other treatises are also attributed to him.

Āruṇi
------------------------------------------
Āruṇi, son of अरुण Aupaveśi, is one of the more important teachers mentioned in the उपनिषद्स्. When he was under-going training in Vedic studies, his गुरु धौम्य once commanded him to stop the water that was leaking out of his fields. आरुणि lay across the breach and stopped it. Hence, he came to be known as उद्दालक (‘One who bound or fastened the bund’). गौतम is another appellation for him. श्वेतकेतु was his son.
He once went to the king प्रवाहण जैवलि and was humble enough to learn about the Pañcāgnividyā or the ‘doctrine of ड़िवे ड़िरेस्’ from him.
When he discovered that his son श्वेतकेतु was puffed up with pride after returning from his teacher’s होउसे, due to Vedic learning, he put him a fundamental question: ‘Have you known that by knowing which, all the unknown becomes known?’ Since श्वेतकेतु did not know and requested him to teach it, आरुणि taught him this esoteric wisdom. (vide Chāndogya Upaniṣad, chapter 6.)

Aruḷnandi
------------------------------------------
Śaivism, centred round the worship of शिव, is a very ancient religious cult of India. शैवसिद्धान्त, also known as Tamil शैविस्म्, is an important contribution to the Śaiva lore of South India. Its basic canonical works were composed by Meykaṇdār, अरुऌनन्दि (also spelt as Aruṇandi), ज्ञान सम्बन्धर् and Umāpati, all of whom lived during the period 13th—14th centuries. These four have been designated as ‘Sanātana Ācāryas’ or ancient teachers.
Aruḷnandi was the family preceptor of the young मेय्कण्डार्. The story goes that puffed up with vanity, he once asked his pupil मेय्कण्डार् about the nature of इग्नोरन्चे. मेय्कण्डार्, the young saint simply looked at the proud questioner himself as if in reply. The teacher immedi-ately realized that he himself had been pointed out as a specimen of इग्नोरन्चे, and, overcome by shame, became a disciple of the young saint, assuming the name अरुऌनन्दि Śivācāriār.
He has written a commentary called Śivajñānasiddhi on मेय्कण्डार्’s basic work Śivajñānabodha which itself is in twelve sūtras or aphorisms. This work is in two parts, the first, ‘Parapakkam,’ refuting other schools of philosophy and the second, ‘Supakkam,’ expounding the fundamentals of his own school. The latter is in verse and is considered to be a commentary on मेय्कण्डार्’s work. Another work, Irupāvirupabtu is also attributed to अरुऌनन्दि.

Aruṇa
(‘the red one’)
------------------------------------------
Aruṇa, the charioteer of सूर्य, the Sun-god, was the first son of the sage कश्यप and विनता. Since her pregnancy lasted too long, विनता impatiently pressed her womb, resulting in the deformity of limbs to the unborn child. So, अरुण was born without thighs. (Hence the name anūru, one without thighs.) He was appointed by the gods as the charioteer of सूर्य. He is red in colour and imparts his hue to the sky as he drives in the chariot.
Garuḍa, the famous mount of विष्णु, is his younger brother. सम्पाति and जटायु the two giant birds mentioned in the Rāmāyaṇa are his sons.
Aruṇa is also the name of a demon killed by the goddess दुर्गा, in her aspect as Bhramarāmbā.

Arundhatī
------------------------------------------
Arundhatī, the famous wife of the famous sage वसिष्ठ, is considered as the paragon of wifely virtues. She was the daughter of प्रजापति कर्दम and देवहूति. अत्रि’s wife अनसूया was her sister and the sage कपिल, her brother. The ṛṣi शक्ति was her son. She was as erudite as her husband and was an ācāryā (preceptor) in her own right.
She is said to exist in the form of a नक्षत्र or a star. The ‘Arundhatī-नक्षत्र’ is identified as the star Alcor, belonging to the Great Bear group.
It is obligatory for newly married couples to see the अरुन्धती नक्षत्र. Since it is very dim and scarcely visible, the priest shows the brighter स्तर्स् nearby and then gradually directs their eyes to the real अरुन्धती. This is known as ‘Arundhatī दर्शन न्याय’ or simply as ‘Arundhatī न्याय.’ It signifies the method of leading from the gross to the subtle, from the known to the unknown, in लोगिच् and philosophy.
Arundhatī is also the name of a medicinal plant used to heal serious wounds.

Aruṇapraśna
(‘the section connected with अरुण [or Sun]’)
------------------------------------------
This is a famous and popular Vedic passage forming the first prapāṭhaka (Chapter) of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka. Since it is mainly devoted to अरुण or the Sun god, it has been named Aruṇapraśna (or Aruṇopaniṣad). It is used extensively in all rituals and religious rites connected with सूर्य or the Sun-god on occasions such as Makarasaṇkrānti, रथसप्तमी and the month of Māgha (January- February).
It is a very long passage involving a variety of subjects. It has 32 anuvākas (sections) each अनुवाक containing some kaṇḍikās (short or long mantras in prose), the total of the latter being 130.
A very brief summary of these anuvākas can now be given:
Anuvāka 1 (3 kaṇdikās)
This अनुवाक is devoted entirely to praising and praying to the deities of waters.
May the deities अग्नि, वायु and सूर्य bring to me the sacred rivers—Gaṅgā यमुना and others.
May the deities of waters give me many sons.
May they destroy all my diseases and troubles.
May the earth protect me.
Anuvāka 2 (4 kaṇdikās)
Four ways of gaining knowledge are stated first.
The concept and the various divisions of time based on the movement of the sun are described next. Time personified as Kālapuruṣa (Cosmic Person of eternity) is portrayed beautifully.
However, time at the mundane level as related to sacrifices is dear to men.
Anuvāka 3 (4 kaṇdikās)
This section deals with the ṛtus or seasons.
The terms mentioned here are:
muhūrta: 48 minutes.
30 muhūrtas aho-rātra, day and night, dina.
māsa: 30 dinas.
ṛtu: 2 māsas.

The three well-known ṛtus described here are:
Vasanta-ṛtu — Spring
Grīṣma-ṛtu — Summer
Varṣa-ṛtu — Rainy season

Their characteristics also are described.
Anuvāka 4 (3 kaṇdikās)
The next three ṛtus are described here. They are:
Śarad-ṛtu — Autumn
Hemanta-ṛtu — Early winter
Śiśira-ṛtu — Winter

In the last ṛtu, people suffer due to scarcity of water.
Anuvāka 5 (2 kaṇdikās)
This describes the greatness of the gods known as ‘Viśvedevas’.
Anuvāka 6 (3 kaṇdikās)
It first describes the effect of the Śiśira-ṛtu (winter) wherein people pay attention to keeping themselves warm, above all other things.
Then it declares that those who perform the rituals prescribed for each of these ṛtus (or seasons) will attain greatness here and become one with सूर्य after death.
Anuvāka 7 (6 kaṇdikās)
There are seven Sūryas or Sun-gods. They are: Āroga, Bhrāja, Paṭara, Pataṅga, Svarṇara, Jyotiṣīmān and Vibhāsa.
The sage कश्यप who lives on the मेरु mountain is considered the eighth सूर्य from whom the seven Sūryas get their power to shine.
Out of these, Āroga gives light and heat to us, of this world.
The others give light to the upper and the lower worlds.
These seven Sūryas are satiated by the offerings given by the sacrificer and give him whatever he needs and wants.
Anuvāka 8 (8 kaṇdikās)
The earth and the sky are supported by विष्णु. They give to the human beings and animals the ड़ोओद् that is needed.
Mṛtyu or death is of four types: पर (highest), avama (lowest), madhyama (middling) and catu (the fourth).
Sūrya is पर-मृत्यु. वायु is madhyama-मृत्यु. Jāṭharāgni (digestive power) is avama-मृत्यु. And, चन्द्र (the मोओन्) is catu or the fourth मृत्यु.
These mṛtyus or deaths are ordained upon people according to their karmas.
There is an interesting description of the various punishments given to the sinners.
Anuvāka 9 (7 kaṇdikās)
This अनुवाक describes that there are eight Agnis, eleven Vāyus, and eleven गन्धर्वस्.
This is followed by a prayer to गौरी, the White One, viz., सरस्वती, the goddess of speech.
All the gods worship अक्षर, the indestructible ब्रह्मन्. They appointed the sage जमदग्नि as the protector of this science of meditation on अक्षर. He created the mantras in metres like गायत्री through which he spread the knowledge of अक्षर.
The section ends with a well-known śāntimantra ‘tacchaṁyorāvṛṇīmahe...’
Anuvāka 10 (7 kaṇdikās)
Major part of this अनुवाक is devoted to the praise of the अश्विन्स्, the twin deities.
Anuvāka 11 (8 kaṇdikās)
Holy ṛṣis perform sacrifices like the सोमयाग which please God वरुण who gives plenty of rains. सोम juice, the main ingredient, is therefore eulogised here.
Next, there is the statement that those who did तपस् to attain higher states were reborn as great sages like वसिष्ठ, अत्रि, Marīca and अगस्त्य.
The famous Gāyatrīmantra is a part of this अनुवाक.
Then there is a beautiful description of परमात्मन् as the origin and inspirer of all.
The next section declares that women who have attained the आत्मन् are really men whereas the ignorant men are women only!
Next, this world is compared to an inverted tree, as described in the उपनिषद्स्. One who realises its ephemeral nature is not afraid of death.
Then comes a short description of the ātmajñāni, man of realisation.
It ends with a special prayer to अग्नि and वायु, the gods of fire and wind, to accept the offerings in the sacrifice.
Anuvāka 12 (5 kaṇdikās)
This अनुवाक is mainly devoted to praising इन्द्र, inviting him to the sacrifice to accept the oblations and cause rain through the clouds.
Anuvāka 13 (3 kaṇḍikās)
It begins with the prayer of the sage to मोथेर् Earth and the Sky (Antarikṣa). He declares that by knowing these, one has no death.
This is followed by a short story of अदिति, the मोथेर् of gods. Her eighth issue—in the form of an egg—was born ‘dead’ and so she abandoned it. It is this ‘dead-egg’ that became the Sun, who is hence called ‘Mārttāṇḍa’.
There is a strong belief that these mantras of this अनुवाक should not be heard by pregnant women since it may cause abortion!
Anuvāka 14 (4 kaṇḍikās)
The Sun, causing the various units of time like ahan or day, ṛtus or seasons, saṁvatsara or year, takes away our life as also our sons and animals. Hence a prayer is offered to him not to do it! Similar prayer is offered to the nakṣatras or स्तर्स् also.
Anuvāka 15 (1 kaṇḍikā)
By meditating on the different aspects of आदित्य or the Sun I can also shine like them. This is what the ṛṣi is telling.
These aspects are: eight वसुस्; eleven Rudras; twelve Ādityas; those who speak truth always; the Maruts or wind gods; the ऋभुस् (a class of shining gods); the विश्वेदेवस्; the Saṁvatsara (the year).
Anuvāka 16 (1 kaṇḍikā)
The ṛṣi declares ‘Being in the company of the eight Sūryas—Āroga, Bhrāja, Paṭara, Pataṅga, Svarṇara, Jyotiṣīmata, Vibhāsa and Kaśyapa—I am also shining like them!’
Then he prays: ‘Like the relationship between सूर्य and waters, let our—my and wife’s—relationship too be unbroken!’ This last prayer is spread over the anuvākas 14 to 18.
Anuvāka 17 (2 kaṇḍikās)
Vāyus or the Wind-gods manifest themselves in eleven pairs (along with their spouses).
Some of these are: Prabhrājamānā, Prabhrājamānī; Vyavadātā, Vyavadātī; वासुकि-vaidyutā, वासुकि-vaidyutī and so on.
The ṛṣi says that he shines in their places through his तेजस् (svatejas) or brilliance.
Anuvāka 18 (1 kaṇḍikā)
There is अग्नि in all the eight quarters. Identifying himself with each, the sage says he too shines brilliantly. Prayer for strengthening the bonds of his मर्रिअगे is also offered.
Anuvāka 19 (1 kaṇḍikā)
There are four narakas or hells in the four intermediate directions. They are: Visarpī in āgneya or south-east; Avisarapī in Nairṛtya or south-west; Viṣādī in īśānya or north-east; and Uttarāpara in north-west.
‘Please protect us from falling into these hells!’—says the ṛṣi.
Anuvāka 20 (1 kaṇḍikā)
This is a prayer to the various deities like Indraghoṣas, वसुस्, Manojavases, Pracetās, Rudras, Viśvakarmā, Ādityas, त्वष्टा, Rūpas to protect the beings in their respective regions.
Anuvāka 21 (3 kaṇḍikās)
This is practically a repetition of the first अनुवाक.
The famous śāntimantra (peace-hymn) ‘oṁ bhadraṁ karṇebhiḥ...’ is added here.
The ṛṣis known as Ketugaṇas, Vātaraśanās and Samāhitāsas are requested to serve or pray to the Jaladevatās or the deities of waters.
Anuvāka 22 (7 kaṇḍikās)
This is the well-known Mantrapuṣpa. See MANTRAPUṢPA for details.
The last part deals with the च्रेअतिओन् of the worlds, the Sun and the सोम juice. It also describes the setting up of the sacrificial fire known as ‘Āruṇaketukāgni’ in which अग्निहोत्र, दर्शपूर्णमास, पशुबन्ध and चातुर्मास्य Yāgas are performed.
Anuvāka 23 (9 kaṇḍikās)
The process of च्रेअतिओन् of the world by प्रजापति (the Creator) from āpas or primeval waters is described first, as also the birth of some sages like Aruṇas and Ketus from his body.
Suddenly there appeared ब्रह्मन् in the form of a Cosmic Tortoise who completed the process by creating the आदित्य (the Sun), अग्नि (the fire), वायु (the wind and इन्द्र (the king of gods). The quarters as also a number of other beings were also produced by Him. Then he entered into his own च्रेअतिओन्. Hence the whole च्रेअतिओन् is ब्रह्मन् Himself. One who realises this enters into ब्रह्मन् or becomes ब्रह्मन्.
Anuvāka 24 (4 kaṇḍikās)
There are four sources of water in nature. They are: megha (clouds); vidyut (lightning); tuṣāra (fog); vṛṣṭi (rains).
There are other sources of water on earth. The water from these sources is used in the Āruṇaketuka sacrifice as follows: Water collected from rain is kept in a container to the east of the sacrificial altar. Well-water is kept in the south. Water collected from small tanks is kept in the west. River water is collected and sprinkled in the direction of north. Water stored in the होउसे in vessels is placed in the middle of the altar. Water from small pits is also collected and sprinkled on the bricks of the altar.
The section ends with the beneficiary results of Āruṇaketuka sacrifice.
Anuvāka 25 (3 kaṇḍikās)
This section describes the method of preparing an altar for the five Vedic fires. Digging a pit, filling it partly with water, spreading a lotus leaf and placing its stems and flowers and bricks over it, the altar is to be built.
Anuvāka 26 (7 kaṇḍikās)
There are ड़िवे ड़िरेस्: Sāvitra, Nāciketa, Cāturhotriya, Vaiśvasṛja and Upānuvakya. The sacrificer can offer oblations into these fires separately as per the desire he wants to be fulfilled such as getting children, acquiring cows, rains, health and destroying the enemies.
The अनुवाक warns human beings not to dirty water nor eat animals living in water like tortoise.
Anuvāka 27 (6 kaṇḍikās)
Worshipping the Āruṇaketukāgni and offering oblations into it as per the rules of the sacrifices can produce various results. Some of them are: Freedom from the effects of even mortal sins; attaining long life and हेअवेन्; realising ब्रह्मन्; driving away evil spirits; destroying inauspiciousness.
It also urges human beings to forsake the terrible attachment to the body.
Anuvāka 28 (1 kaṇḍikā)
This is a prayer to अग्नि to drive away all the evil spirits, including their मोथेर् Vācyā (or Amaṅgala).
Anuvāka 29 (1 kaṇḍikā)
At the instance of the yajamāna (the sacrificer), the ṛtviks (priests) offer a prayer to Parjanya, the rain-god, so that people can have plenty of rain.
Anuvāka 30 (1 kaṇḍikā)
This contains a prayer for the protection and increase of virility.
Anuvāka 31 (6 kaṇḍikās)
The first part contains a prayer to कुबेर-वैश्रवण inviting him to the sacrifice. The second part contains some rituals like giving बलि (sacrificial offering).
This part of the Veda should never be imparted to anyone who is forgetful and callous.
Anuvāka 32 (3 kaṇḍikās)
One who wants to perform the Āruṇa-ketuka sacrifice should observe certain rules and austerities for one year or at least two months.
He has to bathe three times a day. He should beg for ड़ोओद् and eat only once in the day. He has to offer sticks of audumbara wood (Ficus racemosa) in the होम with mantras addressed to eleven deities such as अग्नि, वायु, सूर्य, ब्रह्मा and others with the syllable स्वाहा. होम should be offered to the ṛṣis known as Aruṇas.
Svādhyāya or Vedic studies should be kept up in the forest.
One who observes all these, becomes a tapasvī (sage) and a पुण्य (auspicious person).

Āruṇeyī Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
Known also as ‘Āruṇi-’ and ‘Āruṇika-’ Upaniṣad, it is a minor work belonging to the Sāmaveda. It deals with सṁन्यास or monastic life.
The sage आरुणि goes to the abode of प्रजापति (‘Lord of beings;’ same as ब्रह्मा, the Creator) and asks Him how he can give up all actions. प्रजापति replies that he should give up his family and friends, the holy thread, the sacrificial system and the scriptures that advocate them and the desire for attaining any of the well-known worlds or planes of exis-tence. He should accept सṁन्यास or monastic life. This is the first section.
The next section clearly states that anyone, from any state of life, can take to the monastic life, intense spirit of renunciation being the only criterion. The process of ceremonially giving up the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) and the fires, and the exhortation to study the आरण्यकस् and उपनिषद्स्, follow next.
The third section gives the well-known praiṣamantra, the sacred formula to be repeated thrice, signifying that the aspirant has totally renounced the three worlds. A Vedic prayer for protection, instructions regarding ड़ोओद्, wearing of the loin-cloth and observance of disciplines like ब्रह्मचर्य (chastity), अहिṁसा (non-injury) and सत्य (truthfulness) are given at the end.
The fourth section deals with the conduct of ‘paramahaṁsa-परिव्राजक,’ the highest class of itinerant मोन्क्स्. They should sleep on the ground, use a bowl of clay, gourd or wood for water, give up lust, anger, avarice and other evil passions and constantly move about, all alone, except during the rainy season. (See CĀTURMĀSYA.)
The last section describes the mode of begging, uttering the sacred ‘Oṁ,’ and closes with a well-known Vedic prayer that describes the state of enlightenment of sages.
See also SAṀNYĀSA and UPANIṢADS.
